The Third Plague Pandemic. In 1855, a global resurgence of bubonic plague began in China and spread to every inhabited continent by the early twentieth century, killing an estimated 12 to 15 million people. Unlike earlier medieval pandemics, it occurred in the age of modern science, allowing researchers to identify the plague bacillus and map transmission routes while simultaneously affecting colonized regions disproportionately.

The pandemic began in southern China in Yunnan Province, likely triggered by ecological disruption or expanded rat populations. It spread via trade routes to Hong Kong and eventually the world. India alone lost an estimated 10 million people between 1896 and 1948. The bacterium Yersinia pestis was identified by Alexandre Yersin in 1894, and its flea vector was confirmed by Paul-Louis Simondt, enabling scientific understanding of transmission.

The plague spread in three forms. Bubonic plague caused swollen lymph nodes, pneumonic plague spread through the respiratory system and was highly transmissible, and septicemic plague infected the blood. Pneumonic outbreaks caused rapid, explosive mortality. Colonial port cities—Hong Kong, Mumbai, San Francisco, and Sydney—were hit hardest, exposing the vulnerability of global trade networks and crowded working-class districts.

San Francisco experienced an outbreak from 1900 to 1910 that was suppressed through rat extermination and quarantine, but the disease continued covertly in prairie dog populations of the American West. The pandemic demonstrated the power of microbiology and epidemiology to identify pathogens and understand transmission vectors, ushering in the modern scientific era of disease control.
